result.summary: Pausanias discusses the Sibyls and other inspired prophets, beginning with the rock at Delphi where Herophile chanted. He sets out the rival claims about the two Herophiles, her birthplace, her tomb in the Troad, and then lists later prophetesses and inspired men.

scenes.title: Herophile and the Delphic rock
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes the stone at Delphi and the Sibyl's ancestry, and quotes her verses on her mortal father and Nymph mother.

scenes.title: Marpessus and the Sibyl's tomb
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes Marpessus and the river Aidoneus in the Troad, then Herophile's life, death and tomb in the grove of Sminthian Apollo.

scenes.title: Rival claims and other prophets
scenes.summary: Erythræ claims Herophile as its own, and Pausanias lists Demo, Sabbe, Phaennis, the Peleades and inspired men.

alias_notes.explanation: Title of the prophetess; the Libyans are said to have given the name.
Erythræans say she was so called from well-wooded places being called Idas.

notable_quotes.reason: Famous triple formula of Zeus's eternity, sung by the Peleades of Dodona.
The Sibyl's epitaph, a haunting voice now silent.

analysis.text: Pausanias weighs local claims and evidence about the Sibyls, showing his habit of testing traditions against inscriptions and visits.
Many cities competed to claim the Sibyl, as prophetic prestige brought honour and pilgrims.

legacy.text: The Sibyl tradition fed Roman and later Christian ideas of pagan prophecy, as in the Sibylline Books and medieval art.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias says Sabbe was a Hebrew prophetess, an early Greek reference to Jewish or Sibylline oracles.

language_notes.text: Sibyl was originally a title for prophetic women; the Libyan origin of the name is claimed here by tradition, and Lamia was a Libyan queen in myth.
Her prophecy refers to Helen, whose abduction to Troy caused the Trojan War; 'Asia Minor' here means the Trojan side of Asia.
'Eat' is an old past-tense form, 'ate'; 'eating bread' is a Homeric way of saying he was mortal.
A stade was a Greek unit of about 600 feet (roughly 180 metres), so 240 stades is about 27 miles.
'Sacristan' means a temple keeper, here a female attendant in charge of the sanctuary of Sminthian Apollo.
Hecuba's dream, before Paris's birth, of a firebrand foretelling Troy's destruction is the likely reference.
'Near the Nymphs and Hermes' describes the nearby statues, which the final sentence then confirms.
Idæa is explained as from the old word "Idas" for wooded places, a folk etymology linking her name to Mount Ida-like forests.
Refers to a line in the Herophile oracles, mentioned earlier by Pausanias, about Marpessus and the river Aidoneus; Erythræ rejects it because it ties her to the Troad.
"The Hebrews beyond Palestine" means Jews living outside Palestine; Sabbe's origins were disputed, as the sentence shows.
Chaones were a people of Epirus, in northwestern Greece.
Antiochus seized the Syrian kingdom after Demetrius was captured; this dates Phaennis to the third century BC.
A famous Dodonaean chant, said to be sung by the Peleades, praising Zeus in past, present and future.

context_notes.text: Delphi was Apollo's chief oracle; the rock was a landmark there where the Sibyl was said to have sat and prophesied.
Delos was the island sacred to Apollo's birth, and its people cited her hymn as authority.
Clarus near Colophon, Delos and Delphi were all famous oracular sites of Apollo.
A square Hermes, or herm, was a squared pillar topped with a head of Hermes, common as a boundary or roadside marker.
Cumæ, in Campania, was an early Greek colony in Italy, famous for its Sibyl; Demo is the Cumæan Sibyl in this tradition.
Dodona in Epirus held an ancient oracle of Zeus, where priestesses called Peleiades gave answers.
Bacis, Musæus and Euclus were legendary seers whose oracles circulated in Greece in collected form.

literary_notes.text: Her claim to be Apollo's wife, sister and daughter at once is contradictory, suggesting divine inspiration speaking through her.
The tomb inscription speaks in the first person, letting the dead prophetess address the reader.
A once vocal prophetess is now 'for ever dumb', a poignant contrast between her past and her silence.
The repeated "Zeus was, is, shall be" gives a liturgical rhythm and asserts the god's eternity.
Pausanias speaks as a personal researcher, stating what he has read himself, which lends the catalogue authority.
The closing reflection speculates calmly about the future, ending the catalogue of prophets with a detached, scholarly tone.
